messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: more on K-distributions
parts:
I managed to code up a working fitter for K distributions
using the exp/gamma encoding:

if u ~ exponential(1)
and v ~ gamma(nu,L/nu),

then sqrt(u * v) ~ K(nu,L)

Although it's getting the right answer, the Jacobian
I'm using seems off to me and the whole model's a bit
fishy because of the double sampling on the same parameter.


First, the data simulator and then call in R:

-------------------------------------------------
library('rstan');
N <- 2000;
L <- 1.75;
nu <- 2.5;
u <- rexp(N, 1); # latent nuisance 1
v <- rgamma(N, nu, L / nu); # latent nuisance 2
y <- sqrt(u * v); # y ~ K(nu, L);
fit <- stan(file="estimateK.stan",
data=list(N=N,y=y),
init=0,
iter=500, chains=2);

====================================================

And running it:

----------------------------------------------------
> print(fit,c("nu","L"))
Inference for Stan model: estimateK.
4 chains, each with iter=1000; warmup=500; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=500, total post-warmup draws=2000.

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
nu 2.5 0 0.2 2.1 2.4 2.5 2.7 3.1 123 1
L 1.8 0 0.4 1.2 1.6 1.8 2.1 2.9 121 1

Samples were drawn using NUTS2 at Fri May 31 01:12:04 2013.
=========================================================


With zero-inits, it only takes about 75 warmup iterations
to converge. It takes much longer with diffuse random inits,
but eventually gets there.

Now here's the model in Stan:

----------------------------------------------------
data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector<lower=0>[N] y;
}
transformed data {
vector<lower=0>[N] y_squared;
y_squared <- y .* y;
}
parameters {
real<lower=0> nu;
real<lower=0> L;
vector<lower=0>[N] v;
}
model {
v ~ gamma(nu, L / nu);
y_squared ./ v ~ exponential(1);
lp__ <- lp__ - sum(log(v));
========================================================


First, the model is just the vectorized form of this:

for (n in 1:N) {
v[n] ~ gamma(nu, L / nu);
y_squared[n] / v[n] ~ exponential(1);
lp__ <- lp__ - log(y[n] / v[n]);
}

And there, my reasoning was:

if y = sqrt(u * v),
then u = y^2 / v

and so we can use v as a latent (nuisance) parameter, so that:

if y ~ K(nu,L),
use v ~ gamma(nu, L/nu)
(y^2 / v) ~ exponential(1)

But what's confusing me is the Jacobian.
The inverse transform for the exponential(1)
is

y[n]^2 / v[n],

so I'd think the log absolute Jacobian would be

log |d/dv y[n]^2 / v[n]|

= log |y[n]^2 v[n]^{-2}|

= 2 * log(y) - 2 * log(v)

and because y is a constant, I just drop that term.

But that systematically estimates L to be twice what
it should be, which is why I tried cutting the Jacobian
in half to see what would happen. Now it fits, and I've
tried many different L and nu values, and they all work.

Can anyone point out what I'm doing wrong here on the math
side?

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: more on K-distributions
parts: Here's how I thought it through. Let
u = y^2 / v

So, we have the fact that

f(u,v | ...) = |J| * f(y,v | ...)

where J is the Jacobian matrix of the "bivariate" transformation from (u,v) to (y,v). So, with the independence assumptions,

f(y | ...) * f(v | ...) =

Thus, we have the "4" partial derivatives:

dy / du  = sqrt(v) / (2 * sqrt(u)) dy / dv = sqrt(u) / (2 * sqrt(v))
dv / du  = 0                       dv / dv = 1

Those collectively form J, whose determinant is sqrt(v) / (2 * sqrt(y^2 / v) = v / (2y). So, log(abs(det(J))) = log(v) - log(2 * y) and log(2 * y) is a constant, leaving log(v). But we are dividing by |J| above so that gets negated when we log.

Ben

I was just thinking about this and figured it the other

With

(y^2 / v) ~ exp(1)

I figured I was doing the Jacobian backwards, and what I really

On Fri, May 31, 2013 at 1:16 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
and so we can use v as a latent (nuisance) parameter, so that:

  if    y ~ K(nu,L),
  use   v ~ gamma(nu, L/nu)
        (y^2 / v) ~ exponential(1)

But what's confusing me is the Jacobian.
The inverse transform for the exponential(1)
is

   y[n]^2 / v[n],

so I'd think the log absolute Jacobian would be

  log |d/dv y[n]^2 / v[n]|

  = log |y[n]^2 v[n]^{-2}|

  = 2 * log(y) - 2 * log(v)

it is a bit tricky here to think about transformation as we need to specify distribution for both y and v, data and parameters. 
An easy way for this case is to consider that we need to specify the joint distribution of 
p(y, v, nu) or p(y^2, v, nu), the posterior distribution of (v, nu) up to a constant. 

p(y^2, v, nu) = p(y^2 | v, nu) p(v, nu) 

then p(y^2 | v, nu) = (1/v) * p(y^2 / v | v, nu) 

So the term -log(v) should be added to lp__.
